structure.title: Chapters 1–5 · Childhood without a birth date
structure.text: Douglass begins with information white children commonly possessed about themselves and he was denied. Songs carried back from the Great House Farm, a child's hunger and the disappearance of a relative show how much labour went into keeping enslaved people from knowing their own families and circumstances.

structure.title: Chapters 6–9 · Baltimore and the alphabet
structure.text: Sophia Auld starts teaching the child to read until her husband explains what literacy would cost a slaveholder. Douglass understands the warning from the opposite side. Bread exchanged for lessons and letters copied from the shipyard turn a city into a clandestine school.

structure.title: Chapters 10–11 · Work under Covey and the struggle for freedom
structure.text: Hired out to a man reputed to break difficult slaves, Douglass describes exhaustion so complete he can scarcely use what he knows. His later account of wages, resistance and escape makes careful distinctions between gaining a little power over his labour and owning his person.

structure.title: Appendix · An appendix on Christianity
structure.text: Anticipating readers who may hear an attack on their faith, Douglass distinguishes the religion preached by slaveholders from the Christianity to which he appeals. The particulars of what church members buy, sell and excuse give the distinction its force.

people.name: Frederick Douglass
people.text: The adult writer can explain a system the child knew through food, cold, sound and fear. He preserves the difference. At times he tells us precisely what he could not have understood or known when he witnessed an event.

people.name: Sophia and Hugh Auld
people.text: Sophia's first impulse toward the boy is generous. Her husband's intervention teaches Douglass something about the source of their authority. His account also follows what exercising that authority does to a woman who began by offering help.

context.title: Why an escape narrative withholds information
context.text: A person who publishes the details of a route may expose those who still use it or help others along it. Douglass takes his reader's curiosity seriously enough to argue with it. Silence can be an obligation owed to somebody who has yet to reach safety.

notice.text: Hear the argument about the songs.
notice.why: An outsider might hear the singing as proof of contentment. Douglass remembers hearing and joining it, then describes how its meaning changed for him. The passage asks who has the standing to interpret a sound another person makes under constraint.

passages.quote: as evidence of their contentment and happiness

notice.why: A skilled workman can find a job, negotiate the work and receive the pay himself, then have to surrender it at the end of the week. Douglass gives theft an address, a schedule and a man waiting for the money.

opening: Frederick Douglass hears a slaveholder explain why teaching him to read would make him unfit for slavery. The warning gives him a purpose. Learning opens a world his enslavers need to keep closed, while making his own captivity more painful to understand. Douglass writes about violence, calculated ignorance, and the struggle to recover authority over his body and mind with a precision that refuses the reader comfortable distance. The man whom slavery was supposed to render voiceless becomes an exacting witness against it.
